lesson.title: Boundary Testing: Interrogating the Line Itself
lesson.summary: Boundary testing zooms the edge-case mindset in on the exact thresholds inside a function's comparisons, checking the value right at, just below, and just above each limit, because off-by-one mistakes cluster precisely at those lines.
lesson.body:
You already know the broader habit of edge-case thinking, deliberately testing empty inputs, single-element inputs, and other unusual but valid cases instead of only the inputs that feel typical. Boundary testing takes that same instinct and points it at something more specific: any place in your code where a comparison draws a line, an if statement using less than, greater than, less-than-or-equal, or greater-than-or-equal, is a place where the exact number chosen for that comparison, and whether it uses < or <=, determines the outcome for values sitting right at that line.

These lines are where off-by-one bugs live, mistakes where a comparison should have included the boundary value but excludes it, or the reverse. Writing age <= 17 when you meant age < 17, or the other way around, produces code that behaves identically for every input except the handful of values sitting exactly at 17, which makes these bugs notoriously easy to miss with casual testing and only reliably caught by testing the boundary directly. The systematic approach is to pick three values around every boundary that matters: the boundary value itself, one value just below it, and one value just above it.

```python
def get_ticket_price(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("age cannot be negative")
    elif age <= 12:
        return 8
    elif age <= 17:
        return 12
    else:
        return 15

for test_age in [12, 13, 17, 18]:
    print(test_age, "->", get_ticket_price(test_age))
```

This function has two meaningful boundaries: the line between the child price and the teen price, sitting between ages 12 and 13, and the line between the teen price and the adult price, sitting between ages 17 and 18. Rather than testing some arbitrary child age like 5 and some arbitrary adult age like 40, this loop tests exactly the four values that sit right on those two lines. age 12 satisfies age <= 12, so it returns 8, the child price. age 13 fails age <= 12 but satisfies age <= 17, returning 12, the teen price, confirming the boundary shifted at exactly the right value. age 17 still satisfies age <= 17, also returning 12. age 18 fails both elif checks and falls to the else branch, returning 15, the adult price. The output is:

```
12 -> 8
13 -> 12
17 -> 12
18 -> 15
```

If the second condition had accidentally been written as age < 17 instead of age <= 17, this exact test would expose it immediately: age 17 would fall through to the else branch and incorrectly return 15 instead of 12, a one-value mistake that a broader test using ages like 5, 15, and 40 would never have noticed, since none of those values sit on the boundary where the bug actually lives. That is the whole case for boundary testing, it does not test more inputs than edge-case testing, it tests more precisely chosen ones, aimed directly at the exact lines in the code where mistakes are most likely to hide.
